messages.body_plain:
Dear List,

I am trying to understand if I can use ermg to model my dataset about adoption of an innovation. 
I have a small network of people where each link between A and B represents A influenced B. 
I then have an attribute variable which represent for each node the time of adoption of the innovation.

What I?d like to know is: can I use network measures to predict time of adoption? As far as I have understood, I can use nodes attributes as independent variables and see how they affect the network structure?

but would it be possible to do the contrary? Would it be possible to use network measures to say something about the value of nodes attribute? 

Any reference to literature on this point, or statnet example code will be much appreciated.

Best regards,
Simone

cross-sectional snapshot of a network, Ian Fellows (fellstat.com) has a 
separate program that implements selection/influence models for

If you have longitudinal panel data on the networks, we don't (yet) have 
that functionality built.  But we do have a student working on this for 
his dissertation project, so it's in the works.

best,
Martina

messages.body_plain:
That is the correct reference. The package is currently not in public release as it lacks the documentation necessary for end users. I'm happy to send the package to anyone who would like it with the understanding that it is an active development project. I do plan on doing a release in the next 6mo or so.

The current development does not include continuous nodal attributes (such as those described by Simone), though this is an area which I will be working on this year. One avenue that you might wish to explore is to run a regression (e.g. linear) on the nodal variate, using network based statistics as covariates. For example, the average adoption time of the influencers of each node. A regression of this sort can be thought of as a pseudo-likelihood fit of a social influence model.


Best,
Ian

messages.body_plain:
Hi Rose,

The CEF terms like gw* have 2 parameters.  One of these controls the 
overall magnitude of the effect of a tie forming the configuration of 
interest, the other controls the rate at which this effect decays for 
additional configurations.  If you don't understand what the parameters 
do, spend some time on the Hunter 2007 article, and try playing around 
with the implications in an excel spreadsheet.

In practice, we often don't have enough information in a network to 
estimate both parameters, so we fix the decay term.  If set to 0, only the 
first instance of the configuration counts (so, maximal decay), as we fix 
it to higher values, the decay is smoothed and reduced.

Even if fixed, this is a CEF term.

hth,
Martina

messages.body_plain:
Duncan,

EpiModel may help depending on your question of interest and the structure
of your data. To address your specific questions:

1. Using the epiDCM or epiICM (note: the latest release v0.95 -- available
on CRAN -- has changed the terminology of these non-network stochastic
microsimulation models from SPM to ICM for "individual contact models"
although the core internals remain the same), it is  possible to input a
range of parameters and evaluate which set most closely fits to empirical
disease incidence or prevalence data (I assume you mean this sort of
fitting). The qualitative way of doing this is to choose a combination of
parameters for counterfactual models and see what set best minimizes the
distance to the data. If the deterministic compartmental modeling suits
your research question (which seems unlikely since you want to use network
models, but DCMs are an easy place to start), then this may be performed
with the sensitivity analysis framework of epiDCM (see Section 2.3 of our
Tutorial: statnet.org/EpiModel/vignette/Tutorial.pdf). More complex model
fitting procedures, such as Bayesian melding, are certainly possible with
DCMs, but not currently integrated into EpiModel; it is a potential area of
future software development. I'm not aware of any R package that does
automated melding for epidemic models (because epidemic software itself is
limited in R), although the method could be programmed for your specific
research questions.

2. Our guiding framework for network modeling is to use egocentric data on
contacts (or edges or partnerships) with estimates of the average duration
of those contacts. We rarely have a longitudinal census of a disease-risk
network, and even if we did have such data, we would need a statistical
model to estimate the properties of the data generating process and
simulate that process forward. There are a number of ways to estimate such
a model (see, for example:
http://statnet.org/workshops/SUNBELT/current/tergm/tergm_tutorial.pdf). But
to use a non-egocentric approach in EpiModel, currently it would be
necessary to: 1) use a STERGM to estimate the parameters given your
observed network data; 2) simulate a complete network dynamically to
calculate summary target statistics of interest; then 3) plug those target
statistics into EpiModel with the framework outlined in our EpiModel
tutorial (linked above). One area of future EpiModel development may be
integration of complete network data, but it is not our highest priority
because the data are so rare within epidemiology.

One additional note is that you will likely need to extend the code within
EpiModel to suit your specific research questions, as the built-in models
are relatively simplistic SI-SIS-SIR disease models. The framework for
extension has been outlined for DCMs (see
http://statnet.org/EpiModel/vignette/ExtendepiDCM.html). We will be
focusing our much of our development efforts over the next year to help
facilitate this process of extension for network models.

Finally, just to note that we have established an EpiModel-specific mailing
list, which you are encouraged to subscribe and pose future EpiModel
questions there (although we'll still respond on the statnet list too!).
http://mailman11.u.washington.edu/mailman/listinfo/epimodel

Best,
Sam Jenness

On Fri, 7 Mar 2014, Duncan McPherson wrote:

> I have some data of epidemic diffusion and want to fit a series of 
> models of increasing complexity, hopefully ending up with showing that a 
> STERGM model is the best fit to the data.

Just to be clear, STERGM is a model for estimating the generative 
parameters for a dynamic contact network from observed contact network 
data (and simulating dynamic networks consistent with the observed contact 
data).  It is not a model for inferring this network from data on epidemic 
outcomes, or for estimating the biological parameters of the epidemic 
process.

> 1. Can I use epiDCM or epiSPM to estimate/infer parameters for a SI 
> model from data and then test for goodness of fit?

>From what kind of data?  Contact data?  Epidemic incidence data?  And 
which parameters?  The generative contact network parameters or the 
biological disease paramaters?

> 2. Let?s say I know the exact network of contacts, and want to estimate 
> parameters for epidemic spread over that network from data, is that 
> possible?

Which parameters did you want to estimate?  EpiModel (via STERGM) will 
estimate contact network parameters, but it simulates (not estimates) the 
spread of infection on the resulting network.  You can identify the range 
of epidemic outcomes consistent with the observed network via simulation, 
and you can estimate the summary epidemic statistics from these 
simulations.  But I'm not sure that's what you mean by "estimate 
parameters for epidemic spread"

Hi Jimi,
  I'm very sorry to take so long in responding.

If I'm understanding what is going on with your movie, I think there are 
two different ways to address it.

1) You can specify a two-column matrix of initial.coords as an option in 
the render.par paramter list passed into the render.animation command. 
This will specify a default position for each newly-appearing vertex 
that doesn't have a position defined in a previous slice.  However, the 
same values for each vertex would be applied throughout the movie, so it 
may not work to have it appear exactly where it is going to go if it 
appears more than once.  But I've found it sometimes works nicely to set 
random values that are well 'off screen' so that the vertices will 
arrive onto the layout instead of appearing in the middle.

2) The option that I think is more likely to get the effect you want is 
what we've been calling 'reverse-chaining' -- just running the layouts 
backwards so that vertices will usually appear at the "correct" position 
(for the layout in which they appear).  You can enable this option by 
setting the chain.direction parameter in the compute.animation function 
from 'forward' instead of 'reverse'.


Let me know if either of these approaches works.  If not, maybe you can 
send me the file (if it is not sensitive) and I can try to figure out a 
good set of params (or if there is a bug in ndtv).

If your data above is in a data.frame named theDataFrame, you should be 
able create a network with "Value" as an edge attribute with this command:

net<-as.network(theDataFrame,ignore.eval=FALSE,names.eval='Value',bipartite=30)

This is assuming that vertices with ids 30 and below are in the first 
mode of the bipartite network, and those with ids above 30 are in the other.

> I've googled high and low and searched the
> statnet archeives, but I can't seem to find anything about how to assign
> vertex labels for plotting purposes or attributes for ERGM purposes.

The network help page ?loading.attributes  may have some examples that 
might help.

>
> I presently have attributes (labels/values) etc. in a separate csv
> file.  I'd like to do all the things I have done with single mode
> networks (ie: nodematch, absolute difference etc).  Presently the file
> is composed as such:
>
> ID    Name     Attribute1
>
> 21     Bob         .35
>
> 22     Steve       .31
>
> 23     Sue         .55
> Is there an equivilent to rownames(attributes$names) for bipartite
> networks?  Likewise, is there an equivalent fornet %v%"attributeone" <- attribute$V1?

Bipartite networks use the same attribute assignments as single-mode 
networks, you just need to be careful with the ids as you assign 
attributes, perhaps using the "v" argument to only assign to one mode at 
a time.

Assuming your example above is a data.frame, have you tried:

net%v%"attributeone" <- attribute$Attribute1

This should assign the value of attribute$Attribute1  to an attribute 
named "attributeone" on ALL the vertices of "net"  HOWEVER, the 
correspondence of elements in "attribute" to vertices is by the row id, 
NOT by the ID column.  In other words, if the rows in the attributes 
file are not in the same order as your vertices, the wrong values may 
get assigned.

If you want to use the value of the ID column to determine which vertex 
the attribute gets assigned to, this should work:

net<-set.vertex.attribute(net,attrname='attributeone',value=attribute$Attribute1,v=attribute$ID)

If you have separate tables of attributes  for the vertices in each mode 
of the network, you can use the "v" argument to specifiy which vertices 
get assigned. Note that vertices do not all need to have attributes with 
the same name.

Please let me know if this solves your problem.

Dear Tom, 
It sounds from your description (high probability of tie formation for large or small values, low probability at middle values) as though you can easily do this ?by hand?:  Simply take your nodal covariate, square it, and create a new nodal covariate whose values are the squares.  Then add both covariates to the model using nodecov.

If you want to avoid collinearity, you can try subtracting the mean of the original covariate values before squaring.  Or, if you?re already familiar with the poly() function, you should simply be able to use the output from that function to create the covariates you will first add to the network as new nodal covariates and then add to the model using nodecov.

> library(ergm)
> set.seed(123)
> ntwk <- network(5)
> x <- 1:5
> x2 <- (x-mean(x))^2
> ntwk %v% "x" <- x
> ntwk %v% "x2" <- x2
> ergm(ntwk~nodecov("x") + nodecov("x2"))

 nodecov.x  nodecov.x2  
   -0.1075     -0.1708  

I hope this is helpful.

Dave

Hi, Tom.  Two vertices, i and j, are said to be strongly connected in 
graph G if there exists an (i,j) path in G and a (j,i) path in G.  i and 
j are said to be recursively connected if there exists an (i,j) path in 
G with vertices (i,a,b,...,j) such that its reversal (j,...,b,a,i) is 
also a path in G.  Strong and recursive components, then, are maximal 
sets of vertices that are respectively strongly and recursively 
connected.    (See also ?component.dist.)  Your test case is weakly and 
strongly connected, and hence has one component under these notions of 
connectedness.  It has no recursively connected paths, however, and 
hence the maximum component size is 1 (yielding three components).

Hope that helps!

Hi, Tom.  Your example has a spanning cycle - thus, for every pair of 
nodes (i,j), one can get from i to j or from j to i.  Specifically, 
let's number the nodes in your case as 1,2,3, with 1->2, 2->3, and 
3->1.  Then e.g., we can get from 1 to 2 by the 1->2 edge, and from 2 to 
1 via the path 2->3->1.  (The same holds, mutatis mutandis, for all 
other pairs.)  This highlights a potentially counterintuitive aspect of 
strong connectivity: it requires no mutuality at all, and the two 
connecting paths for a given vertex pair can be entirely disjoint 
(excepting their endpoints)!  But if one is interested in flows that 
need not traverse any particular path, strong connectivity can be a 
useful concept.

Hope that helps!

-Carter

Hello, I have a network consisting of 6,584 vertices and 716,401 directed edges. I am using R 3.03 in RStudio with the latest version of statnet on a Windows 8 64 bit Server with 512 GB of RAM and an Intel Xeon E5-4650 @ 2.70GHz processor. 


My independent variables (for now) include vertex attributes node_status_count (positive continuous) and followers_count (non-negative interval). I would also like to control for mutual ties and triangles. 


# import data 

> el=read.csv(file.choose(),header=TRUE) # read a .csv file 
> atts <-read.csv (file.choose(), stringsAsFactors=F, strip.white=T, as.is=T) 
> n=network(el,matrix.type="edgelist",vertex.attr=atts, vertex.attrnames=colnames(atts),directed=TRUE) 
> n 


# set control object 


> maxNumDyads=network.size(n)^2 
> c=control.ergm(MPLE.max.dyad.types=maxNumDyads, MCMC.burnin=1000000, MCMC.samplesize=300000, parallel=4) 


# this works with MCMC 
> t02 <- ergm(n ~ edges + mutual + triangle, control=c,verbose=TRUE) 


# this works if maxNumDyads is set to a very large number, e.g. maxNumDyads=network.size(n)^3 
> t03 <- ergm(n ~ edges + mutual + triangle + nodecov("norm_status_cnt"), control=c,verbose=TRUE) 



# the full model does not work, returning a "too many unique unique dyads" error 
> t04 <- ergm(n ~ edges + mutual + triangle + nodecov("norm_status_cnt") + nodecov ("followers_count"), control=c,verbose=TRUE)

I reviewed related posts on the statnet archives, e.g. https://mailman13.u.washington.edu/mailman/htdig/statnet_help/2010/000675.html.
